abstract: We present OpenTac, a novel sensor and a full-stack ecosystem for tactile skins that are highly customizable, scalable, and readily deployed in downstream robot control and learning applications. Our core contribution is twofold. First, we develop a scalable resistive tactile skin with a structured deformable overlay that converts tangential loading into spatially varying pressure. Differential responses across neighboring "taxels" support decoding of local shear vectors, and the common-mode response encodes normal force. Second, we provide a highly customizable sensor design tool that is able to automatically generate fabrication files for these tactile skins from 2D outlines and developable 3D surfaces, including from abstract descriptions such as text (e.g., "design a sensor for a size 9 shoe insole"). We develop an ecosystem around the OpenTac sensor, including the CAD design tool, a sensor simulator, cross-sensor transfer, and fast/adaptive data acquisition. We demonstrate the broad applicability of the OpenTac-CAD sensor design tool by designing and fabricating more than 30 sensors across a variety of robot embodiments. We characterize the three-dimensional tactile fields produced by OpenTac with a commercial, high-precision force/torque sensor. We demonstrate the broad applicability of 3D tactile sensing across contact-rich feedback control and manipulation policy learning on four real-world robot embodiments. Additionally, adaptive acquisition enables kilohertz-rate partial readouts, exceeding full-array raster scanning on the same sensor by 19.2X at 16 sampled taxels per update for a 1024-taxel skin. We provide all hardware, software, and result videos are at opentac.github.io

sections.body: The paper argues that tactile sensing research is limited by how hard skins are to customize. Existing skins such as FlexiTac provide only normal-force (1D) estimates and need manual redesign for each geometry. Prior sensors are sampled at 30 to 100 Hz with raster scanning. The authors present OpenTac, with a CAD design tool (OpenTac-CAD), a simulator (OpenTac-Sim), cross-sensor transfer (OpenTac-Transfer), and adaptive acquisition (OpenTac-Xampling). For a 32×32 skin, adaptive acquisition of sparse contacts reaches 1286 Hz, against 67 Hz for full-array scans.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing tactile skins are hard to customize and sample slowly, so OpenTac offers a design tool, simulator, transfer, and fast readout.

sections.body: The related work groups prior systems by transduction, customization, simulation, and acquisition. It cites optical, magnetic, capacitive, and resistive sensors, and notes that Sun et al. infer load direction from four piezoresistive cells under a bump. It describes AnySkin as relying on a predefined electronic layout and eFlesh as relying on separately supplied magnetometer electronics. For simulation, it lists TACTO, Taxim, DiffTactile, TacEx, Taccel, and HydroShear. For acquisition, it lists event-driven hardware and adaptive subsampling of dense arrays. Table 1 compares these systems on automatic design, shear sensitivity, and cost per unit.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior systems address transduction, customization, simulation, and acquisition separately; OpenTac aims to unify these from robot geometry.

sections.body: Each OpenTac skin has a piezoresistive film under a printed bump strip, with each bump over a 2×2 group of taxels. Normal force is read as a common-mode sum, $h_{z}$, while shear is read from differential sums, $h_{x}$ and $h_{y}$. An optional affine map calibrates these readings to force units. The manifest stores each taxel's physical center, scan indices, footprint, and bump group. It is shared by four modules: OpenTac-CAD, OpenTac-Sim, OpenTac-Transfer, and OpenTac-Xampling. The text states that 31 sensors were designed in OpenTac-CAD and fabricated with a flexible-PCB printing service.
sections.heading: The OpenTac Ecosystem
sections.headline: The piezoresistive skin uses a deformable bump overlay to decode shear, and four modules share one manifest file.

sections.body: Experiments cover generated designs, force accuracy, simulation fidelity, policy learning, transfer, and adaptive readout. The 31 boards were generated with zero design-rule violations, and every fabricated board was functional. OpenTac-CAD covers 75%, 90%, 89%, 87%, and 93% of the YUBI, UMI, LEAP, Robotiq, and B2 regions, against 57%, 90%, 79%, 87%, and 93% for the rectangular baseline. Force estimates against OptoForce reach R² of 0.95, 0.93, and 0.96, with RMSE of 0.11, 0.16, and 0.15 N. On the SO-101 plug insertion task, OpenTac-3D-full reaches 70% against 54% for its pose-only baseline. Adaptive acquisition reaches 1286 frames per second with 16 sampled taxels per update, against 67 frames per second for raster scanning.
sections.heading: Experimental Evaluation
sections.headline: All 31 fabricated boards passed design-rule checks, and the sensor's force estimates correlated with a reference sensor.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes OpenTac as an ecosystem spanning robot surface geometry, fabricated skins, manifest-driven simulation, cross-sensor transfer, and high-speed acquisition. It lists four limits. The flexible PCBs are not stretchable, and mesh-derived layouts need surfaces that flatten into developable patches. Piezoresistive sensing has hysteresis, drift, and temperature dependence. Adaptive acquisition trades spatial completeness for update rate, so larger contact regions need larger sampling budgets. Simulated signals are deformation proxies, and transfer is evaluated on normal-contact shape, not on force accuracy or sim-to-real policy performance. All hardware, firmware, software, and data are released.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The authors list limits: boards are not stretchable, surfaces must be developable, sensing drifts, and sampling trades completeness for rate.

sections.body: The appendix lists contribution statements for each author. Roles include conceiving the project and leading the manuscript, developing the CAD, transfer, and adaptive acquisition tools, co-developing the simulator, leading sensor characterization and calibration, running load-cycle tests, and running policy learning on the SO-101 and bimanual YAM robots. One author designed and fabricated a tactile glove using OpenTac sensors. Others ran robot experiments on the DexMate Vega Pro or coordinated sensor design across experiments. Supervisors provided research guidance and strategic advice.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists each author's contributions, covering hardware, software, sensor characterization, policy learning, and supervision.
